title: Does California Make You Happy?
text:
Many Americans picture California as a place where life is better, mostly because of the weather. In the late 1990s David Schkade and Daniel Kahneman tested whether Californians actually are happier and whether people elsewhere think they are.

They surveyed nearly 2,000 students at large universities in the Midwest (in Michigan and Ohio) and in Southern California. Students rated their own satisfaction with life overall and with specific aspects such as climate, job prospects, safety and cultural opportunities. Some were also asked to imagine a student similar to themselves living in the other region and rate that person's satisfaction.

Overall life satisfaction was the same in both regions. Californians were much happier with their climate, as expected, but it did not translate into a happier life. Yet both groups predicted that a student like themselves would be happier in California. When people thought about the difference between the regions, the obvious difference, the weather, came to mind and seemed decisive. In reality, everyday life in both places was dominated by things that were the same: studies, friends, money, plans for the future.

Schkade and Kahneman called this a focusing illusion. Kahneman later summed it up in one line: nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
lesson: When a single feature makes a change look wonderful, such as a new city, job or house, ask how much of your ordinary day it will really touch. Most of life stays the same.
location: Universities in the Midwest and Southern California, USA
source: Schkade, D. A., and Kahneman, D. (1998). Does living in California make people happy? A focusing illusion in judgments of life satisfaction. Psychological Science, 9(5), 340-346.
